definition: Computer-aided translation (CAT), also referred to as computer-assisted translation or computer-aided human translation (CAHT), is the use of software, also known as a translator, to assist a human translator in the translation process.
details: The translation is created by a human, and certain aspects of the process are facilitated by software; this is in contrast with machine translation (MT), in which the translation is created by a computer, optionally with some human intervention (e.g. pre-editing and post-editing). CAT tools are typically understood to mean programs that specifically facilitate the actual translation process. Most CAT tools have (a) the ability to translate a variety of source file formats in a single editing environment without needing to use the file format's associated software for most or all of the translation process, (b) translation memory, and (c) integration of various utilities or processes that increase productivity and consistency in translation.

explainer.lead: Computer-assisted translation gives human translators software that handles repetitive and organizational work while they make the translation themselves. It matters because translators can work more consistently across file formats and reuse earlier translations without handing the creative and linguistic decisions to a machine.

tiers.eli5: Imagine writing a story in a special notebook that remembers sentences you wrote before and suggests them when they appear again. Computer-assisted translation is like that notebook for translators: it helps with the busywork, but the person still chooses the words and writes the translation.
tiers.practitioner: A translator typically opens several supported source formats in one CAT editing environment and works with translation memory and other productivity utilities. Translation memory can improve reuse and consistency, but its suggestions still require human judgment; CAT should also not be confused with a machine-translation workflow built around pre-editing or post-editing computer output.
tiers.paperLevel: Computer-assisted translation is a human-authored translation process in which software facilitates selected tasks, whereas machine translation is computer-authored translation with optional human intervention. CAT tools characteristically provide a common editing environment for multiple source formats, translation memory, and integrated utilities for productivity and consistency; their scope is facilitation of the translation process rather than autonomous generation of the translation.

explainer.example: A translator is localizing a product manual and reaches the sentence “Save your changes.” The CAT tool finds that the same sentence was translated in an earlier manual and offers that translation through translation memory; the translator checks that it fits the new context, accepts or edits it, and continues in the same editor even though other chapters came in different file formats.

usedIn.name: Human translation workflows
usedIn.detail: Software supports the translator while the translator remains responsible for creating the translation.

usedIn.name: Multi-format translation projects
usedIn.detail: Different source file formats can be translated in one editing environment without relying on each format's associated application.

usedIn.name: Consistency-focused translation
usedIn.detail: Translation memory and integrated utilities help translators reuse previous work and maintain consistent output.

explainer.intuition: The software acts as a skilled workspace rather than the translator: it organizes files, recalls earlier translations, and supplies helpful utilities while a person makes the linguistic decisions.
howItWorks: The translator brings supported source files into a single CAT editing environment.
The tool presents the material for translation and draws on translation memory for relevant earlier translations.
The human translator creates or revises the translation, using integrated utilities to support productivity and consistency.
The completed human-authored translation is produced without requiring most of the work to be done in each source file's original application.
explainer.whyItMatters: CAT reduces repeated effort and helps maintain consistency while preserving human authorship. A shared editing environment and integrated utilities also make translation across multiple file formats more manageable.
misconceptions: CAT is not machine translation: in CAT, the human creates the translation, while in MT the computer creates it.
A CAT tool does not remove the translator's judgment; translation-memory suggestions and other assistance still need to be evaluated in context.
CAT tools are specifically concerned with facilitating the translation process, not merely with any software a translator happens to use.

diagram.caption: The CAT environment supplies text, remembered translations, and utilities; the human translator produces the final translation.
